note: Frozen in Phase 0 with schema.json; version 2 adds the figures of the feature loops, tools and code, version 4 the example catalog's own answers about each example, version 6 the values of the figures kept separate, and version 7 the source's own account of its loops. The data stream implements these definitions; the dashboard and the methodology page show them. A change here is a contract change, and bumps version.

periods.interval: half-open [start, end), on calendar days in the timezone, from the original UTC timestamps (never relabelled UTC days)
periods.note: All time is the default while history is short. A bounded period is offered only for period metrics. Deltas against an earlier period need comparable coverage in both; a missing baseline is unavailable, and a zero baseline with new activity is shown as new, never as a percentage.

metrics.label: Estimated model usage
metrics.definition: Sum of the token-priced usd of every model call in the cohort, at the list prices of pricingAsOf.
metrics.coverage: Priced calls of all calls in the cohort; unpriced calls add nothing and are counted as missing.
metrics.notes: An estimate from token counts, not a bill. Client-reported usage, unattributed usage and the hypothetical cost without caching are other figures, never added to this one.

metrics.label: Model calls
metrics.definition: Number of model API calls in the cohort, subagent calls included once.
metrics.coverage: Sessions with a metrics file of all sessions in the index.

metrics.label: Input cache reuse
metrics.definition: sum(cache_read_tokens) / sum(input_tokens + cache_read_tokens + cache_write_tokens) over the cohort, weighted by tokens; never an average of ratios.
metrics.coverage: Calls with token counts of all calls in the cohort.
metrics.notes: Unavailable when the denominator is zero. Cache reads are context processed again, not new input. Thinking tokens are part of output and play no part here.

metrics.label: Completed verification jobs
metrics.definition: Number of verification jobs with a result whose finishedAt falls in the period, passed or failed.
metrics.coverage: Results with a finishedAt of all results.
metrics.notes: Not filtered by model: too few jobs link to the session that submitted them. A passed job is one that ran as its steps expected; it may well have refuted a change.

metrics.label: Median verification duration
metrics.definition: Median wallSeconds of the completed jobs in the period with a valid (positive, finite) value, shown with the number of jobs it is taken over.
metrics.coverage: Jobs with a valid wallSeconds of the completed jobs in the period.
metrics.notes: Per job. Summed job time is not factory wall time: jobs run in parallel.

metrics.label: Recorded changes
metrics.definition: Distinct jj change ids in the rollup at the source revision; trace-publication housekeeping counted apart.
metrics.coverage: Changes with at least one session of all changes.
metrics.notes: A total at the revision, not changes per period: the rollup has no commit times.

metrics.label: Examples in the catalog
metrics.definition: Examples in examples/index.json at the source revision, by origin (constructed, real-world), verdict, vacuity and freshness.
metrics.coverage: Examples with a verdict of all examples.
metrics.notes: A stock, never examples per period. The pages use the words of the project's own page for the catalog's verdicts: a violation is refuted, a verified change is established, and an unverifiable one is left open. Where the catalog gives an example no single verdict, its label is read for the catalog's marks (✗, ✓, ⚠): one kind of mark is that verdict, more than one kind counts as more than one verdict, and no mark is an example not proved yet. An established label is not a claim of a current, non-vacuous proof: freshness may be unknown and a proof may be vacuous. The catalog also says of each example whether the module's existing unit tests passed on the same patch, and how severe the change would be if it shipped unnoticed. Both are the catalog's statements, counted as written (overview.catalog), over the examples that have them. Most examples were constructed for the catalog, with the systems and tests they change. An example's own result file says what its verdict rests on: the existing tests' task and the tests that failed, the first counterexample or a model checker's trace, and how long the attempt took where it is recorded. That text is carried as written and cut at 320 characters.

metrics.label: Share of usage by model
metrics.definition: Each raw model id's usage_usd divided by the cohort's usage_usd.
metrics.notes: Describes where usage went; says nothing about which model is better. Different task mixes make models incomparable.

insights.template: {share} of input tokens were read from cache ({scope}).
The median verification job took {duration} ({n} jobs, {scope}).

figures.label: Feature loop runs
figures.definition: Run records of feature-loop.sh under llm-dlc/traces/{session}/runs/ at the source revision: one per start of a loop. A cycle is one pass through the loop's brief that ends in a commit, as the record lists it.
figures.coverage: Runs whose session has a prompts table of all runs with a record.
figures.notes: Loops run before 2026-11-06 left no record and are not counted. A campaign groups a brief's parallel streams with the loop that merges them (config/loops.json).

figures.label: Loops, runs and cycles, as the source adds them up
figures.definition: The source's own loop statistics, llm-dlc/traces/loops.json at the source revision: every run of its loop script and of the verification loop, with each run's cycles, commits, verification jobs, time and estimated usage. A run with a published record is read from the record; a run from before 2026-11-06 is read from its session's prompts; a session whose every prompt is /run-verification is one run of the verification loop. A commit is a cycle's when the session made it during one of the cycle's turns. Active time is the time a model call or a tool call was under way.
figures.coverage: Every run the source lists. It says how many it read from records and how many from the prompts of sessions that left none.
figures.notes: Read as the source states it and checked to add up: its categories, its loops and its runs each give its totals. The loop a person ran by hand before the script existed is counted with the moonshots and told apart by its kind. A prompt typed into a run is one that is not the loop's own. The clock of every run is drawn from this account: a bar from a run's start to its end, with a notch where each cycle that committed ended, and a new stretch where no loop had run for six hours. The pace of commits over a stretch counts the loops that write code; the verification loop's commits of results in the same hours are said apart. The run records these pages also read cover only the runs that left one, so only those runs open on the clock, and the campaigns show fewer runs than this account.

figures.label: Prompts typed by a person during a run
figures.definition: Prompts the trace records as typed input that start inside a run's window and match none of the loop harness's or the agents' own message templates, plus interruptions (config/loops.json).
figures.notes: Zero means nobody typed into the session between the run's start and its end. It doesn't mean nobody was watching, and it doesn't count what a person did before starting the run (writing the brief) or after it (reviewing the result). Messages from other agents are counted apart.

figures.label: Work inside a run
figures.definition: Model calls, tool calls, output tokens, estimated usage and agent time of the prompts that start inside a run's window; commits are the distinct recorded changes committed inside it, trace-publication housekeeping left out. In a total, a change committed in two runs, a stream's and then the loop's that merged it, counts once.
figures.notes: Agent time is the time the session spent answering prompts, pauses left out. Run time is the clock from a run's start to its end. Runs in parallel add up, so neither is factory wall time.

figures.label: Who set off the work
figures.definition: Each tool call is given to the sender of the latest prompt before it in its session: the loop's script, a person (typed text or an interruption), or other (a slash command, a message from another agent, anything before a session's first prompt). A notification that background work finished keeps the driver it follows. Tool calls per prompt a person typed divides a day's tool calls by the prompts and interruptions a person typed that day (config/loops.json).
figures.coverage: Every session with a tools table; it doesn't need a run record, so it covers the loops run before 2026-11-06 too.
figures.notes: The sender is read from the start of a prompt's text, so a loop prompt whose template isn't listed counts as a person. A day with no typed prompt has no ratio. A person's prompt often starts or restarts a loop, so the two are not rivals.

figures.label: Compactions, and the sessions that had one
figures.definition: A session is one Claude Code conversation, with everything after a compaction. The source's rollup, llm-dlc/traces/metrics.json at the source revision, gives each session its compactions, its agent time, its tool calls, its estimated usage and the largest context it reached. A session counts as compacted when it has at least one compaction. Agent time is the span from a prompt to the last record of its turn, added over prompts. A model at work and a tool at work are the time at least one such call was under way, so calls made together are not counted twice.
figures.coverage: Sessions the rollup gives a count of compactions.
figures.notes: Read as the source states it, and checked: the sessions' compactions add up to its total. The shares say where the work was, not that compaction caused it: a session that works for hours is the one whose context grows. Tool time comes from timestamps, so it includes time waiting for a person to approve a call. The source's logs leave out the compaction calls themselves, so estimated usage does not include what compacting cost.

figures.label: What made a call write to the cache anew
figures.definition: The source's cache events, by its own cause (specification.md, Cache events). A call starts an event if it read under half of the previous call's context, which means the cached context was lost, or if it wrote 20,000 tokens or more with the context intact. The cause is the first that applies: a session or subagent started, a compaction came before the call, the model or the effort level changed, the cache expired (the last call was longer ago than an hour, or five minutes where the session writes no 1-hour entries), the log does not say, or the call took in one large input.
figures.notes: The cost of a write is its tokens at the list price of a cache write. Above a cache read is that cost less what reading the same tokens from cache would have cost. Read again later is what the later calls in the same window paid to read a large input again. These are parts of estimated usage, not a figure beside it, and they are not all cache writes: a call that adds a little to an intact context starts no event.

figures.label: Tool call success
figures.definition: Tool calls that returned without an error, divided by all tool calls. A failed call is one of: the command ran and exited non-zero (exit); the harness refused the call, for invalid input or a pattern it blocks (rejected); a person or the permission classifier said no (denied); any other error.
figures.coverage: Sessions with a tools table of all sessions in the index.
figures.notes: A non-zero exit is often the tool working: a test that fails, a search that finds nothing. Rejected calls are the closest thing here to a model's own mistake. Models do different work, so their rates say nothing about which model is better.

figures.label: What followed a failed tool call
figures.definition: For each failed tool call, whether the next tool call in the same session, by start time, succeeded. A streak is failed calls in a row within a session. Hours into a run and loops under way are counted for calls made inside a recorded run only: the time since that run started, and the number of recorded runs whose window holds the call.
figures.notes: The next call is not always a retry of the failed one: the trace doesn't link them. Calls made in parallel, or by a session's subagents, are ordered by when they started.

figures.label: Lines of code added
figures.definition: Lines added in files whose extension config/code.json lists as a language, summed over every commit reachable from the source revision, by git's numstat with renames followed. Lines removed and the lines in the tree at the revision are counted the same way.
figures.coverage: Commits whose change id the traces record of all commits.
figures.notes: Only a snapshot made from a git checkout has this. Docs, JSON, logs, receipts and traces are counted apart and are not code. Merge commits and binary files add nothing.

figures.label: Share of added code still in the tree
figures.definition: Lines of code in the tree at the source revision divided by lines of code ever added.
figures.notes: A coarse measure of rework: it can't tell a line rewritten the next day from one removed on purpose, and a line that was changed counts as one removed and one added. Code still standing by the day it was written splits it by age.

figures.label: Code still standing, by the day it was written
figures.definition: git blame -w -M of every code file at the source revision gives each line the commit that wrote it. A day's surviving lines are the lines blamed to that day's commits; the rest of what the day added has since been rewritten or removed.
figures.notes: Whitespace-only changes and lines moved within a file keep their first commit. A line edited in any other way counts as rewritten. A commit is never credited with more lines than it added. It says how much was reworked, not when or why.

figures.label: Output tokens per line of code
figures.definition: Output tokens of every model call divided by lines of code added.
figures.coverage: As lines of code added, and model calls.
figures.notes: An upper bound on what a line took: the same tokens also wrote the docs, briefs, commit messages and commands. Thinking tokens are part of output. Estimated usage per line divides the same way.

figures.label: Output tokens per line, change by change
figures.definition: For each recorded change that has a commit: the output tokens the rollup gives it (the model calls up to its commit) divided by the lines of code its commit added. The middle change is the nearest-rank median over the changes that added code and were given output tokens; one in ten lies under the 10th percentile and one in ten over the 90th.
figures.coverage: Committed changes the rollup gives a cost for of all commits with a change id.
figures.notes: A change that adds no code (docs, briefs, data) has no ratio and is counted apart. Tokens spent before a change's first commit in a session, such as reading and planning, are given to that change. A change is marked as a loop's when it was committed inside one of the loop's recorded runs.

separate.label: Client-reported usage
separate.note: Claude Code's own figure, written when a session stops, summed over the sessions that have one. The source's logs leave some calls out, namely compactions and side calls, so this is not the estimate under another name; it is shown beside the estimate for the same sessions.

separate.label: Unattributed usage
separate.note: The part of client-reported usage that no call in a session's log explains, as the source adds it up session by session.

separate.label: Cost without caching
separate.note: Hypothetical: the same priced calls at the same list prices, as if nothing had been read from cache. No call was made that way.
